en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 37, the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.

Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Blessed One:

“In what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu, in brief, liberated by the destruction of craving, one who has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate conclusion—the best among gods and humans?
“Here, Lord of the Devas, a bhikkhu has heard:
‘All phenomena are not worth adhering to.’”
And so it is, Lord of the Devas, that when a bhikkhu has heard:
"All phenomena are not worth adhering to," he directly knows all phenomena;
having directly known all phenomena, he fully understands them; and having fully understood all phenomena, whatever feeling he feels—

Whether it be pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, he dwells contemplating dispassion in those feelings, he dwells contemplating cessation in those feelings, and he dwells contemplating relinquishment in those feelings.
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

It is in this way, Lord of the Devas, that a bhikkhu is, in brief, liberated through the destruction of craving; he has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and reached the ultimate consummation—he is the best among gods and humans.

Then Sakka, Lord of the Devas, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him with his right side toward him, and vanished right there.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was sitting not far from the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
"Has that yakkha understood the Blessed One’s speech and rejoiced in it, or has he not?"
"What if I were to find out whether that yakkha has understood and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, or not? Then,
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—
Just as one might stretch out an arm, or bend in an arm that had been stretched out, even so, having vanished from the Eastern Park in Migāra’s Mother’s Mansion,

he reappeared among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Now at that time, Sakka, lord of the devas, was enjoying himself in the Ekapuṇḍarīka Garden, fully provided and endowed with five hundred celestial musical instruments.
Sakka, lord of the devas, saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna coming from afar.
Upon seeing him, he withdrew those five hundred divine musical instruments and approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
"Come, dear Moggallāna! Welcome, dear Moggallāna!"
"It has been a long time, dear Moggallāna, since you made this occasion for coming here.
Sit down, dear Moggallāna; this seat is prepared.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sat down on the prepared seat.
Sakka, lord of the devas, also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As Sakka, lord of the devas, was sitting there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to him:
“In what way, Kosiya, did the Blessed One speak in brief about liberation through the destruction of craving?”
“It would be well if we too might have a share in hearing this discourse.
“Venerable Moggallāna, we are indeed very busy and have much to do—
not only with our own affairs, but also with the affairs of the Tāvatiṃsa gods themselves.”
Moreover, dear Moggallāna, that which is well heard, well grasped, well attended to, and well retained quickly disappears.
Once upon a time, dear Moggallāna, a battle between the gods and the asuras took place.
In that battle, dear Moggallāna, the gods were victorious and the asuras were defeated.
"Thus, dear Moggallāna, having completely conquered that battle and emerged victorious, I returned from there and had the palace named Vejayanta built.
Dear Moggallāna, the Vejayanta palace has one hundred towers.
In each tower there are seven hundred gabled chambers."
"In each gabled chamber there are seven celestial nymphs;
for each celestial nymph there are seven attendants.
Would you like, dear Moggallāna, to see the beauty of the Vejayanta Palace?"
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna consented by remaining silent.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, and the Great King Vessavaṇa, placing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in front of them, approached the Vejayanta Palace.
There, Sakka’s female attendants saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna coming from afar.
Seeing him, feeling abashed and ashamed, they each entered their own private chambers.
Just as a daughter-in-law feels abashed and ashamed upon seeing her father-in-law,
even so did the female attendants of Sakka, lord of the devas, feel abashed and ashamed upon seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and they each entered their own private chambers.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, and the Great King Vessavaṇa made the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna walk back and forth and wander about in the Vejayanta Palace, saying:
"Behold, dear Moggallāna, this delightful beauty of the Vejayanta Palace;
behold, dear Moggallāna, this other delightful beauty of the Vejayanta Palace."
“This [abode] of the venerable Kosiya shines, as befits one who has performed merit in the past.
Even when people see some beautiful thing, they say:
‘How wonderful, sir! It shines like that of the Tāvatiṃsa gods!’”
“This indeed suits the Venerable Kosiya, as it does for one who has performed merit in the past.
Then, it occurred to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“This yakkha dwells far too negligently.”
"What if I were to terrify this yakkha?
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna performed such a feat of supernormal power that he made the Vejayanta Palace tremble, shake, and quiver with his big toe.
Thereupon, Sakka, lord of the devas, the Great King Vessavaṇa, and the Tāvatiṃsa devas were struck with a sense of wonder and amazement, thinking:
“It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
Such is the great psychic power and great majesty of the ascetic, that he can make this divine abode shake, tremble, and quiver with his big toe!
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, perceiving that Sakka, lord of the devas, was moved with emotion and his hair stood on end, said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
“But how, Kosiya, did the Blessed One speak in brief on liberation through the destruction of craving?
It would be well if we too might have a share in hearing this discourse.
“In this case, dear Moggallāna, I approached the Blessed One; having approached, I [addressed] the Blessed One...”
Having paid homage, I stood to one side. Standing to one side, venerable Moggallāna, I said this to the Blessed One:

“To what extent, Bhante, is a bhikkhu, in brief, liberated by the destruction of craving, having reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and realized the ultimate consummation—the best among gods and humans?
When this was said, venerable Moggallāna, the Blessed One said this to me:
“Here, Lord of the Devas, a bhikkhu has heard:
‘All phenomena are not fit for adherence.
If, Lord of the Devas, a bhikkhu has heard this...”
“All phenomena are not worth adhering to.

Thus, he directly knows all phenomena; having directly known all phenomena, he fully understands them; having fully understood all phenomena, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, dwells contemplating dispassion in those feelings, dwells contemplating cessation in those feelings, and dwells contemplating relinquishment in those feelings.

Thus, dwelling in those feelings contemplating impermanence, dwelling contemplating fading away, dwelling contemplating cessation, and dwelling contemplating relinquishment, he does not cling to anything in the world.
Not clinging, he is not agitated; being unagitated, he personally attains nibbāna.
He understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."

"To this extent, Lord of the Devas, a bhikkhu is, in brief, liberated through the destruction of craving; he has reached the ultimate goal, attained ultimate security from bondage, lived the ultimate holy life, and realized the ultimate consummation—he is the best among gods and humans.
"In this way, dear Moggallāna, did the Blessed One speak to me in brief regarding liberation through the destruction of craving.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the words of Sakka, Lord of the Devas—just as...
Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
even so, having vanished among the Tāvatiṃsa devas, he reappeared at the Migāramātupāsāda in the Eastern Park.
Then, not long after the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had departed, the attendants of Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
“Is that Blessed One your teacher, dear sir? “He is not my teacher, dear sir;
he is my venerable co-practitioner, Mahāmoggallāna.”
“Gains for you, dear sir! Well obtained by you, dear sir, that you have a fellow-celibate of such great psychic power and such great majesty.
Oh, surely that Blessed One must be your teacher!”
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to the Blessed One:
"Does the Blessed One recall, Bhante, having spoken in brief to a certain well-known and highly influential yakkha about liberation through the destruction of craving?"
“I recall, Moggallāna, that Sakka, lord of the devas, approached me;
having approached, he paid homage to me and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Moggallāna, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to me:

‘To what extent, Bhante, is a bhikkhu, in brief, liberated through the destruction of craving—the one who has reached the ultimate goal, the one who has attained ultimate security from bondage, the one who lives the ultimate holy life, the one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, the best among gods and humans?’”
When this was said, Moggallāna, I said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
"In this case, lord of the devas, a bhikkhu has heard:
'All phenomena are not worth adhering to.'"
And so, Lord of the Devas, when a bhikkhu has heard this:
"All phenomena are not worth adhering to," he directly knows all phenomena;

having directly known all phenomena, he fully understands them; and having fully understood all phenomena, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—[he dwells contemplating its impermanence, its fading away, and its cessation].
Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in those feelings, he dwells contemplating dispassion in those feelings, he dwells contemplating cessation in those feelings,
and he dwells contemplating relinquishment in those feelings. Dwelling thus contemplating impermanence, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment in those feelings,
he does not cling to anything in the world.
Not grasping, he does not tremble; not trembling, he personally attains final nibbāna.
He understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

To this extent, Lord of the Devas, a bhikkhu is—in brief—liberated through the destruction of craving, one who has reached the ultimate goal, one who has attained ultimate security from bondage, one who lives the ultimate holy life, one who has reached the ultimate consummation, the best among gods and humans.
"Thus indeed, Moggallāna, I recall having spoken in brief to Sakka, lord of the devas, on liberation through the destruction of craving.
This is what the Blessed One said.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was satisfied and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayasutta, the seventh, is finished.
